The skeleton is a hard tissue that determines the ultimate shape, size, arrangement, and
features of the body.
During embryonic and postnatal development, skeletal cell types, such as chondrocytes and
osteoblasts, attain their diversified and essential functional traits and produce specialized
tissues.

Introduction
Our understanding of the genetic, cellular, and molecular processes governing skeletal
development in mammals has considerably improved in recent years because of the
rapid progress in innovative research tools. Discovery of cell lineage tracing tools,
reporter mice, and single-cell genomic and transcriptomic platforms have revolutionized
the field of developmental biology. In lineage tracing, a single cell is labeled in such a
manner that the label is transmitted to the cell’s progeny, resulting in a set of labeled
clones. This method not only provides information about the number of progenies of the
founder cell but also their location and status of differentiation. Used in classical
developmental biology, lineage tracing is increasingly applied to stem cell research and
in modeling cellular heterogeneity in disease conditions (Resource 1; Figure 1). Similarly,
reporter cell and mice models have been developed to identify a set of genes encoding
detectable proteins for rapid screening of cells, in which the genome had been
manipulated via genetic engineering. This method enables the detection of molecular
events induced by physiologic or pharmacologic manipulation (Figure 2). Recently,
genome-wide profiling approaches have begun to uncover the molecular programs and
transcriptional landscapes that drive developmental processes. Particularly, technical
advances that enable genome-wide profiling of thousands of single cells have provided
the tantalizing prospect of cataloging cell type diversity and developmental dynamics in a
more robust manner (Resource 2; Figure 3).

Biomedical research in recent decades has provided important insights into mechanisms
by which skeletal tissues develop and grow during embryonic and postnatal life. This
research also informs how skeletal tissues acquire their organization and structure
during development and growth. It also determines how skeletal cell types, such as
chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and osteocytes, attain their diversified and essential
phenotypic functions (Resource 3; Figures 4 and 5).

System development, in general, and skeletal development, in particular, are complex
yet synchronized processes in which various aspects of development, growth, repair,
and homeostasis coordinately interact. Despite originating from a single cell, various
stages of joint development engage different cellular processes, cell types, gene
signatures, and expression patterns that culminate in development of a mature tissue
with unique cellular, molecular, biomechanical, and functional characteristics. Cells
participating in the development process have the capacity to differentiate into a specific
path, and check-and-balance system is in place to strictly streamline the developmental
process with the utmost accuracy and precision. Various tissues, such as cartilage and
bone, develop during various stages of skeletal system development. The
musculoskeletal system tissues, such as bone, muscle, and cartilage, are derived from
mesoderm, with neural crest contributing to some tissues. Therefore, mesodem forms
nearly all the connective tissues of the musculoskeletal system. Cartilage, bone, and
muscle cells differentiate and form mature functional tissues that allow for mobility of
the musculoskeletal system.1
Development of Synovial Joints
Synovial joint development follows condensation, interzone formation, and cavitation.

Condensation is a process that results from embryonic stem cells without an increase in cell
proliferation and serves as a prechondrogenic mesenchyme at the site for prospective joints.
Interzone cells participate in joint formation, and this zone acts as a signaling center.
The cavitation step is characterized by selective high-level synthesis of hyaluronan by
interzone cells and presumptive synovial cells.

Development of Synovial Joints
The synovial joints are the largest joints in the body and are made up of various tissues
(synovium, cartilage, ligaments, etc.) enclosed within a sheath known as the capsule. The
synovial joint facilitates the articulation between two or more skeletal elements. Synovial
joint development can be broadly classified into two developmental steps: condensation
and interzone formation, and cavitation. For easier understanding of these steps, the
condensation and interzone formation step has been separated into two distinct yet
overlapping steps (Resource 4; Figure 6).

localization of growth differentiation factor-5 (GDF-5)–lineage cells. Top, Localization of
GDF-5–lineage cells in a murine hindlimb. GFP = green fluorescent protein. Bottom,
Trichrome staining shows cell density and morphology during joint formation. n = 6 per
time point. Scale bars: 100 μm. F = femur, M = meniscus, S = synovium, T = tibia.

Condensation

Condensation
The cells that contribute to the skeletal elements of the embryonic limb are derived from
the lateral plate mesoderm. These cells migrate into the limb field and undergo a
phenomenon termed pre-cartilaginous condensation. The bones of the limb form from
these mesenchymal condensations, which differentiate into a cartilage anlagen. The
cartilage anlagen, of the respective future bones, continues to be separated by
mesenchymal condensations. These remaining condensations are the interzone, and the
cells express growth differentiation factor (GDF)-5. The interzone is the site of
presumptive joints. In the cartilage anlagen, chondrocytes undergo maturation, and
growth plates form at each end of the long bone. Conversely, the mesenchymal
condensations at the interzone form joint tissues and structures.2 The condensation
process at the interzone is mediated by several signaling molecules, such as cell
adhesion molecules. A transforming growth factor (TGF)-ß superfamily member, GDF-5 is
highly expressed in the condensing mesenchyme and developing joint. The form of the
condensation varies according to the element type being formed. For example,
condensation appears as a continuous branching structure in long bone elements that
are opposed to each other (eg, humerus). Conversely, other elements, such as the
carpals, arise individually as discrete entities and expand toward each other.3
Interzone Formation

Interzone Formation
The interzone cells actively participate in joint formation and give rise to all joint
structures, such as articular cartilage, synovial lining, and intra-joint ligaments. The

11/31

cartilaginous differentiation takes place at the end of the long bone elements. Between
each of the long bones is a non-cartilaginous region known as the interzone (Resource
5). The interzone serves as an important signaling center for the opposing elements, and
the interzone cells share expressions of GDF-5.
Joint Cavitation

Joint Cavitation
After interzone formation, cavitation of the joint occurs. This process is driven by
selective, high-level synthesis of hyaluronan by interzone cells and presumptive synovial
cells. In addition, as the interzone disperses during enlargement of cavity, the synovial
cavity and articular cartilage develop. After the cavity has been initiated, the surfaces of
the opposing cartilage rudiments undergo gradual shape morphogenesis so that,
eventually, the ends of the two bones form a functioning, friction-minimizing contact
surface (ie, a synovial joint).4
Development of Cartilage
Cartilage development occurs from progenitor cells via differentiation and interzone
formation.
Cartilage at developmental stages provides a template for bone formation.

Development of Cartilage
Chondrogenesis, or cartilage formation, is a dynamic cellular process that involves
mesenchymal cell recruitment and migration, condensation of progenitor cells, and
chondrocyte differentiation. The articular cartilage forms from cells of the interzone. The
mesenchymal interzone cells produce an extracellular matrix (ECM) rich in type I
collagen, hyaluronan, tenascin, and fibronectin. The differentiation of these cells into
articular cartilage involves a change in the extracellular composition. ArticularSEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001001
12/31

chondrocytes then produce cartilage-specific type II, type IX, and type XI collagen and
large chondroitin sulfate–rich proteoglycan, or aggrecan. The expression of type I
collagen is then turned off. Cartilage formation is tightly controlled by cellular
interactions with the surrounding matrix, GDFs, and other environmental factors that
initiate or suppress cellular signaling pathways and transcription of specific genes in a
temporal-spatial manner. In mature articular cartilage, TGF-ß is necessary for
maintenance and homeostasis of the tissue.
Development of Bone
Two major types of bone formation occur: intramembranous bone formation and
endochondral ossification.
Intramembranous Bone Formation
Intramembranous bone forms without a cartilaginous intermediate, with differentiation of
mesenchymal progenitors directly into osteoblasts.

Intramembranous Bone Formation
Some of the most obvious structures derived from the paraxial mesoderm are bones.
Bone formation takes places via a series of sequential events (Resource 6). After
gastrulation, the ectoderm and mesoderm give rise to migratory mesenchymal cell
populations. After committed toward the osteogenic lineage, they activate key
osteogenic transcription factors. These cells are responsible for the synthesis of osteoid,
the organic component of the bone matrix. The continuous matrix deposition and
calcification separate osteoblasts in the bone matrix, where they become osteocytes. A
subset of undifferentiated mesenchymal cells remains at the bone periphery and form
the periosteum, a tissue that lines the bone surface.5 Periosteal mesenchymal cells have
high osteoblastic differentiation potential and are a reservoir of progenitor cells that are
important in fracture healing and bone regeneration. Intramembranous bone formation

occurs in areas of the pelvis and skull. Appositional bone growth along the periosteum of
long bones also occurs via intramembranous ossification.
Endochondral Ossification
In endochondral bone formation, new bone forms on a calcified cartilaginous template. In the
first stage, primary bone formation occurs on the cartilage template. This bone is composed of
disorganized woven bone matrix. Subsequently, the cartilage template and the woven bone
matrix are resorbed by osteoclasts and replaced by mature lamellar bone.

Endochondral Ossification
Long bone growth occurs via endochondral ossification, a process through which
immature cells in the growth plate undergo proliferation and differentiation with
formation of a calcified matrix at the site of primary bone formation. In addition to the
physis, or growth plate, this process also occurs at the epiphysis, the cuboidal bones of
the carpus and tarsus, and at the cartilaginous end plates of the vertebral bodies.
During chondrogenesis, committed mesenchymal cells condense into compact nodules
and differentiate into SOX9-positive cells.6 SOX9 is a transcription factor that induces the
expression of cartilage-specific type II collagen and aggrecan. As development
progresses, SOX9-positive cells proliferate rapidly, leading to the growth of the cartilage
anlagen. Proliferative chondrocytes organize into columnar stacks and begin to enlarge
and mature into hypertrophic chondrocytes that lack type II collagen expression but
extensively express type X collagen. These cells secrete matrix vesicles, which act as
nucleation centers that allow the cartilage template to calcify. As calcification continues,
diffusion of nutrients through the calcified matrix decreases, leading to secretion of pro-
angiogenic and osteogenic growth factors into the ECM. The ingrowth of blood vessels in
combination with cartilage-resorbing cells and periosteal osteoprogenitors ultimately
lead to replacement of cartilage by bone tissue.7,8 The remaining chondrocyte cell
population within the cartilage anlagen organizes into the growth plate, a functional
cellular unit containing resting, proliferative, pre-hypertrophic, and hypertrophic

longitudinal growth through adolescence, at which time hormonal changes cause
involution of this tissue. Endochondral ossification remains in adulthood in bone
regenerative processes, including fracture healing.
Stem Cells Involved in Joint Development
Stem cells, embryonic and adult, are specialized cells with potential for self-renewal and
differentiation along various lineages.
Cell-cell interaction is critical to embryonic development because it coordinates stem cell self-
renewal, cell fate decisions, cell migration, and the organization of cells into tissues.

Stem Cells Involved in Joint Development
Stem cells are specialized cells that are primarily characterized by their potential for self-
renewal and differentiation along multiple lineages. Stem cells can be broadly classified
as embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells. Embryonic stem cells originate from the
inner cell mass of blastocysts and are known to exhibit pluripotency because of their
ability to differentiate along these three lineages: endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.
Conversely, adult stem cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and hematopoietic
stem cells exhibit limited differentiation potential and, therefore, are called multipotent
stem cells. During development, the potential of stem cells for differentiation often is
restricted because the cells reside as quiescent progenitors in a tissue-specific manner.
The tissue-specific cells are thought to maintain tissue homeostasis; however, this
principle does not hold true for all tissues. For example, in the articular cartilage, the
presence of progenitor cells has remained questionable until recently because of limited
healing potential of the articular cartilage. Conversely, bone marrow–derived stem cells
possess chondrogenic potential and, if stimulated, such as via microfracture surgery,
help repair cartilage; however, the repair tissue often is fibrous cartilage, which is
inferior in structural qualities compared with native hyaline cartilage. Hyaline cartilage
exists as a transitional stage tissue during embryonic skeletal development. Although
recent studies have established the presence of progenitor cells in articular cartilage,

these cells are reduced in number with aging, limiting their regenerative potential. These
presumptive progenitor cells express stem cell surface markers; possess differentiation
potential along multiple lineages, such as bone, cartilage, and fat; and are known to
exhibit self-renewal capability (Resource 7). Despite the recent identification of true
stem/progenitor cells in articular cartilage, this tissue has little capacity for healing or
regeneration postinjury.
Cell-cell communication is integral during embryonic development. Communication
between cells coordinates stem cell self-renewal, cell fate decisions, cell migration, and
the organization of cells into tissues. During development, the condensation stage cell-
cell interaction is of paramount importance, particularly for chondrogenesis. Before
condensation, mesenchymal cells begin to produce an ECM rich in hyaluronan and type I
collagen that impairs intimate cell-cell interaction. During condensation, an increase in
hyaluronidase activity is noted with a decrease in hyaluronan in the ECM. Hyaluronan is
thought to facilitate cell migration, and the increase in hyaluronidase and subsequent
decrease in hyaluronan allows for close cell-cell interactions. The establishment of cell-
cell interactions is presumably involved in triggering one or more signal transduction
pathways that initiate chondrogenic differentiation. Two cell adhesion molecules
implicated in this process are neural cadherin and neural cell adhesion molecule. These
molecules are expressed in condensing mesenchyme, then disappear in differentiating
cartilage, and later are detectable only in the perichondrium. Perturbing the functions of
neural cadherin or neural cell adhesion molecule causes reduction or alterations in
chondrogenesis in vitro and in vivo, further supporting a role for these cell adhesion
molecules in mediating the mesenchymal condensation step. In addition to cell-cell
interactions, cell-matrix interaction also is important (Resource 8).
Signaling Cues in Development
Predominantly via analyses of their distribution, several signaling molecules have been
implicated in skeletal development.
The Wnt-ß-catenin signaling pathway is one of the evolutionary conserved communication
systems that regulates embryonic development.

Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-2 and GDF-5 are members of the TGF-ß superfamily, which
play a pivotal role in controlling skeletal development.
BMP-2 regulates the formation of the dorsoventral and anteroposterior axes.
GDF-5 is one of the earliest genes expressed in the embryonic joint interzone destined to form
a synovial joint.
Wnt Signaling

Wnt Signaling
Wnt proteins are secreted growth factors that regulate the proliferation and
differentiation of stem and progenitor cells during embryonic development and during
adult tissue homeostasis in multicellular animals. To date, several functionally divergent
Wnt-based signaling pathways have been identified. One of the most well-characterized
and well-studied pathways is the Wnt-ß-catenin pathway. This pathway is commonly
known as the canonical Wnt signaling pathway. Wnts are a family of growth
factors/ligands that bind to specific cellular receptors, resulting in activation of the
transcription factor ß-catenin. ß-catenin–dependent gene expression programs are
involved in several important cellular functions, including the renewal, differentiation,
and proliferation of stem and progenitor cells. Conversely, the Wnt activated non-
canonical pathways function independent of ß-catenin and have been described to
target small GTPases of the Rho family to control cell polarity and cell movement, or to
act via heterotrimeric G proteins to control calcium ion signaling (Resource 9).
The Wnt-ß-catenin signaling pathway is one of the evolutionary conserved
communication systems that regulates embryonic development. It involves Wnt ligands
that are released by Wnt-producing cells and that act over various ranges to influence
neighboring Wnt-responsive cells. Wnt-ß-catenin signaling is instrumental for defining
the dorsoventral and anteroposterior body axes in multiple animal species.10,11
Paramount to these patterning events, exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of the Wnt-ß-
catenin transcriptional programs is modulated via the action of secreted antagonists,
epigenetic regulation, and the actions of different T-cell/lymphoid enhancement factors,
which are co-factors associated with ß-catenin binding to DNA. Wnt-ß-catenin signaling
also is integrated with other developmental pathways. In addition to an early role in

establishing the embryonic body axes, Wnt-ß-catenin signaling also plays an important
role later in development and growth of various tissues. For example, the synovial joint
interzone cells express Wnt-14, which is important in the development of non-
chondrogenic tissues in the synovial joint.
Wnt-ß-catenin signaling is essential for normal bone homeostasis in the developed
skeleton. Wnt-ß-catenin signaling induces bone formation. The US FDA–approved
biologic monoclonal antibody, romosozumab, is a treatment option for osteoporosis and
enhances bone formation by blocking the activity of sclerostin, a naturally occurring Wnt
inhibitory molecule. In fact, mutations in low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein
5, the Wnt receptor, result in human genetic diseases. An inactivating mutation leads to
reduced ß-catenin signaling and results in osteoporosis pseudoglioma syndrome, which
is characterized by low bone mass. Conversely, activating mutations of low-density
lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 result in a high bone mass phenotype.
TGF-ß Super Family

TGF-ß Super Family
The TGF-ß super family is mainly comprised of the TGF-ßs, and two other major family
members, namely BMPs and GDFs. BMPs and GDFs are considered key players that
control skeletal development because gain- and loss-of-function studies of BMPs and
GDFs in mice revealed changes in skeletal development from defective cartilage
development; some members of the BMP family induce skeletogenesis and stimulate
endochondral bone formation; and BMPs and GDFs have the potential to promote
chondrogenesis.

BMPs are multifunctional growth factors that belong to the TGF-ß superfamily. Currently,
more than 20 BMPs have been identified, making these proteins the largest group of
proteins within the TGF-ß superfamily. BMPs are considered necessary for various
developmental processes, such as neurogenesis, somite formation, and osteogenesis.
Within the BMP family of proteins, BMP-2 was the first BMP to be characterized and has
been extensively studied (Resource 10). BMP-2 plays a pivotal role not only during
embryonic development but also postnatally in processes such bone homeostasis and
remodeling. Specifically, BMP-2 plays a role in digit formation and activation of
osteogenic pathways by increasing the expression of runt-related transcription factor 2,
a key transcription factor in osteogenesis and bone formation.
BMP-2 performs several prominent roles during skeletal development. It is involved in
somite formation and somatic chondrogenesis, particularly in the vertebral and axial
skeleton. In addition, BMP-2 is involved in the formation of digits. BMP-2 supports
programmed cell death to initiate apoptosis in distal limbs, allowing for the formation of
digits; lack of BMP-2 leads to the malformed digits.12 Importantly, BMP-2 is required for
proper osteogenesis, chondrogenesis, and adipogenesis during development.13 BMP-2
acts as a ligand and binds to serine/threonine kinase receptors on the cell surface to
activate the Smad or non-Smad pathways that lead to bone, cartilage, and fat
development. Knockout or suppression of BMP-2 expression impairs the normal
formation of these cells and tissues.14 BMP-2 is a key regulator at various stages of
skeletal tissue development and demonstrates its multi-functionality. During synovial
joint development, the interzone expresses BMP-2 and BMP antagonists, such as noggin.
Loss of noggin expression or continuous overexpression of BMPs results in joint fusion.

The role of GDF-5 in the development of appendicular skeleton originates from GDF-5
mutation studies showing defective development of appendicular skeleton, short stature
malformed joints and digits because of mutation in the GDF-5 gene and modulation of
initial stages of chondrogenesis; however, the mechanism of the manner in which GDF-5
governs skeletal development is not fully understood despite having been extensively
explored. Studies have shown that overexpression of GDF-5 during chick limb
development increased the number of chondrocytes and promoted cell adhesion, a key
determinant of chondrogenesis, resulting in an increase in length of the skeletal
elements. GDF-5 overexpression also resulted in increased size of early cartilage
condensation and later developing skeletal elements within the epiphyseal cartilage
adjacent to its expression within the joint interzone.15,16 Therefore, it appears that GDF-
5 plays a role during two stages of development (ie, during the early condensation stage
and later during skeletal element formation) and via two different mechanisms (cell
adhesion during initial stages and cell proliferation during later stages of development).
The role of GDF-5 in skeletal development is not limited to chondrocyte proliferation and
cartilage condensation but also extends to numerous other processes. For example,
GDF-5 is known to promote sympathetic axon growth and branching and makes a
distinctive regional contribution to the establishment of sympathetic innervation.17
Studies using Gdf5-Cre mice to ablate specific floxed target genes in interzone cells have
shown that the behavior and function of interzone cells are regulated by multiple
mechanisms, including Wnt/ß-catenin signaling and cell surface/matrix macromolecule
interactions.18,19

Adult mammals possess little to no limb regenerative capability; however, specific
musculoskeletal tissues, such as bone, have regenerative potential postinjury.
Tissue regeneration involves the differentiation of tissue progenitor cells, with multi-lineage
potential, into a functional reparative tissue.

Skeletal Regeneration and Development
Extensive regeneration of complex tissues generally occurs in organisms other than
mammals. For instance, hydra and planaria can regenerate their entire bodies from a
small fraction of their tissues. Likewise, vertebrates such as newts and salamanders can
regenerate limbs or other structures after amputation. The regenerative potential in
mammals is limited. Deer and moose can shed and re-grow their antlers. Complete
cartilage regeneration occurs in ear wounds in rabbits and in certain strains of mice;
however, articular cartilage regeneration is limited. Human neonates can regenerate a
fingertip; however, this is lost in later childhood and adolescence. Although tendons and
ligaments heal, typically healing occurs with scar formation, and some ligaments, such as
the anterior cruciate ligament, lack the ability to heal. An exception is bone, which can
undergo bone regeneration and fracture healing with the production of new bone.
Therefore, the focus of scientific study has been defining methods to enhance the
regeneration potential in adult tissues. One approach involves the use of stem cells to
leverage their multipotent potential and differentiation along multiple lineages. An
additional aspect of stem/progenitor cells is that they secrete factors that influence
neighboring cells to differentiate and promote repair/regeneration. Stem cells may aid in
the regeneration of articular cartilage, a tissue with no regenerative potential. The
degeneration of articular cartilage represents an ongoing challenge at a clinical and basic
science level. Tissue engineering and regenerative medicine using stem/progenitor cells
have emerged as valid alternatives to classical reparative techniques but with limited
success.

Mesenchymal Stem Cells
Although MSCs can be isolated from numerous adult tissues and organs, two sources
remain prominent in the literature: bone marrow and adipose tissues. Irrespective of the
source, MSCs are multipotent progenitor cells that possess self-renewal potential and
can differentiate into multiple lineages, including adipocytes, osteoblasts, chondrocytes,
and myocytes.20 MSCs have been widely used in tissue engineering during cell
transplantation in animal models of cartilage lesions and osteoarthritis management. In
large animal models of cartilage lesions or osteoarthritis, cartilage regeneration resulted
from tissue engineering using specific biomaterials and MSCs, indicating its promise for
clinical application.21 In small animal models, MSCs combined with biomaterials also
facilitated hyaline-like cartilage formation. Transplantation of MSCs encapsulated in self-
assembled peptide hydrogels showed chondroprotection and reduced subchondral
bone mineral density in rat osteoarthritis models.22
Although bone marrow MSCs often are used in orthopaedic applications, including joint
injection and injection into bone healing sites, the number of MSCs in a bone marrow
aspirate is limited. Studies have shown that only 55 cells out of 1 million nucleated cells
aspirated from bone marrow have osteoblastic potential. Therefore, whole-bone marrow
aspirate has limited bone regenerative potential.23

Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
One of the remarkable discoveries in the past 20 years has been the ability of
differentiated adult cells to be reprogrammed into a stem cell with unlimited
proliferative potential and self-renewal, similar to embryonic stem cells. Dr. Shinya
Yamanaka, an orthopaedic surgeon–trained scientist, was a recipient of the 2012 Nobel
Prize in Medicine for this discovery. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) may
be a valuable source for cell-based regeneration given their capacity to self-renew and
potentially differentiate into all cell types of adult tissues. Therefore, iPSCs are a suitable

alternative for tissue engineering applications, considering that the cells transplanted
into the patients would be directly differentiated from iPSCs generated by
reprogramming their own somatic cells. In addition, human embryonic stem cells and
iPSCs provide a system for studying human embryonic development and human
diseases and a framework for the production of large quantities of differentiated cells
that can be transplanted for regenerative medicine or tissue engineering applications.
The directed differentiation of such iPSCs into specialized cells in culture requires the
sequential activation of the same signaling pathways that occur during embryonic
development. Insights gained from these developmental approaches have guided
strategies for using growth factors and/or inhibitors to steer differentiation of progenitor
cells toward a specific tissue fate.24 The potential of human iPSCs to regenerate cartilage
is being investigated in preclinical in vivo studies, but they have not been used in human
clinical studies to date. Development of new and reproducible protocols for iPSC
chondrogenic/osteogenic differentiation and efforts to minimize donor variability may
eventually lead to their use in many fields, such as tissue engineering, drug screening,
and modeling of various diseases related to cartilage or even bone (Resource 12).
Signaling Pathways in Regeneration

Signaling Pathways in Regeneration
The derivation of human embryonic stems cells and iPSCs has provided a system for
studying human embryonic development and human diseases and a framework for the
production of large quantities of differentiated cells that can be transplanted for
regenerative medicine or tissue engineering applications. The directed differentiation of
such iPSCs into specialized cells in culture follows the same principles underlying
embryonic development. Therefore, insights gained from developmental biology have
guided strategies for using growth factors and inhibitors of developmental signaling
pathways to maintain pluripotency or steer cell fate toward the desired lineage with
increasing efficiencies.24

Joint Diseases and Development
Developmental abnormalities may influence a specific region or multiple regions of the
skeleton.
Developmental abnormalities may involve a specific tissue and often are hereditary.

Joint Diseases and Development
A major risk factor for osteoarthritis is an imperfect joint structure that ranges from the
obvious defects of hip dysplasia to subtle alterations resulting from mutation of a
developmental gene. Participation of a gene associated with osteoarthritis in the
formation of an imperfect joint may occur during development and may affect the ability
of mature cartilage to be repaired.
Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis
GDF-5 plays a key role in various developmental stages and in different processes
throughout developmental stages. GDF-5 is involved in the progression of joint diseases,
such as osteoarthritis. Studies have shown that allelic variants at the GDF-5 locus have
been linked to osteoarthritis risk25 and suggest that this gene plays key roles in
maintenance of joint homeostasis because its expression has been detected in the adult
cartilage of humans and mice. Studies also have revealed that GDF-5 expression is
increased in stressed cartilage and in newly forming cartilage during tissue remodeling
after knee injury26 (Resource 13).

The morphology of the hip joint is first determined during embryogenesis, at which time
a series of flattened mesenchymal cells of the joint interzone form and define the
boundary between the acetabulum and the proximal femur. Although this interzone
provides progenitor cells to form hip joint structures, such as cartilage, ligaments, and
labrum, neighboring cells give rise to the bony elements. Over the course of late prenatal
and early postnatal development, hip morphology matures, and after it is mechanically
loaded, the various structures undergo a remodeling phase. Changes in this process may
lead to tissue abnormalities resulting in non-physiologic joint loading and, consequently,
and increased risk of joint instability, injury, or osteoarthritis.27 Hip joint development is
particularly relevant clinically because the most commonly presenting condition
resulting from abnormal fetal joint morphogenesis is developmental dysplasia of the hip
(DDH). DDH is a condition in which hip joint morphogenesis does not proceed correctly
and occurs if the juvenile hip joint is unstable, partially dislocated (subluxated), or
completely dislocated. The condition is associated with an incidence as high as 1 in 100
newborns,28 and if management is not administered or is unsuccessful or if DDH goes
undetected, early-onset osteoarthritis ensues. An enhanced understanding of the
sequence of events in the morphogenesis of hip joint development in animal models is
key to advancing understanding of DDH (Resource 14).
GDF-5 also is a major risk locus for hip osteoarthritis, dislocation, and DDH; however, its
mechanism of action in hip disease has yet to be elucidated. Some studies have reported
several distinct GDF-5 synovial joint regulatory enhancers, many of which are
downstream of the GDF-5 gene that harbors risk variants related to hip osteoarthritis,
DDH, and dislocation. Recent research27 indicates that GDF-5 loss results in considerable
dysmorphologies related to hip instability, developmental dislocation, injury, and
osteoarthritis. Mechanistic research further shows that downstream regulatory
sequences of the GDF-5 gene drive stronger and ubiquitous prenatal hip gene
expression and uniquely control GDF-5 gene expression in the postnatal hip. This
regulatory structure is functionally important because downstream sequences are
capable of restoring GDF-5 loss-of-function phenotypes to normal and, therefore,
increase our understanding of the association of GDF-5 in hip pathologies. A recent
human Genome-Wide Association Study meta-analysis suggested that variations in the
